intro.text: Two hundred patients come into a clinic. One hundred really have the disease. One hundred are healthy.

scan.text: An AI model checks each of them, and says one of two things: alarm, or no alarm.

tp.text: Of the hundred sick patients, the model raises the alarm for ninety. Those are true positives.

fn.text: It misses ten. They are sick, but the model stayed quiet. False negatives. These are the dangerous ones.

tn.text: Of the hundred healthy patients, ninety-five get no alarm. True negatives.

fp.text: And five get an alarm they did not need. False positives.

grid.text: That is the confusion matrix. The columns are the truth. The rows are what the model said.

sens.text: Sensitivity looks down the sick column. Of everyone who is truly sick, how many did we catch? Ninety out of a hundred. Ninety percent.

spec.text: Specificity looks down the healthy column. Of everyone who is truly healthy, how many did the model clear? Ninety-five percent.

ppv.text: P P V reads across the alarm row. When the model raises an alarm, how often is the patient really sick? Ninety out of ninety-five. About ninety-five percent.

npv.text: And N P V reads across the no-alarm row. When the model stays quiet, how often is the patient really healthy? Ninety-five out of a hundred and five. About ninety percent.

tip.text: Here is the trick to remember. Sensitivity and specificity start from the truth. P P V and N P V start from what the model said.

cost.text: Which one matters most depends on the cost of each mistake. If missing a sick patient is dangerous, you need high sensitivity. If false alarms waste time and cause worry, look at specificity and P P V.
